questions.q: What is the core difference between blue-green deployment and canary deployment?
options: Blue-green always costs less than canary
Blue-green validates a fully deployed, idle second environment and cuts over all at once; canary gradually shifts a percentage of real traffic to the new version
Canary requires two full environments while blue-green only needs one
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: Blue-green trades gradual exposure for a single atomic cutover between two complete environments, while canary ramps traffic incrementally.

questions.q: In a Kubernetes-based blue-green setup, how is the cutover actually performed?
options: By deleting the blue Deployment entirely
By patching the Service's selector to point at the green Deployment's labels instead of blue's
By rebuilding the green container image
By restarting every pod in both deployments
questions.explain: Cutover changes routing, not what's deployed — patching the Service selector redirects traffic to the already-running green Deployment.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say blue should keep running after cutover rather than being decommissioned immediately?
options: Kubernetes requires at least two deployments to exist at all times
So that rollback is as fast as cutover — reverting the selector or traffic weight back to blue, which is still warm and ready, not something that must be rebuilt
Because green cannot serve traffic without blue also running
Decommissioning blue immediately is technically impossible
questions.explain: Keeping blue alive during a soak period preserves a fast, no-rebuild rollback path if green shows a problem after cutover.

questions.q: What is the main cost tradeoff of blue-green deployment compared to canary?
options: Blue-green requires manual approval gates and canary does not
Blue-green requires running two full production-capacity environments simultaneously during the overlap window
Blue-green cannot be automated with YAML
Blue-green is always slower to roll out than canary
questions.explain: Running a complete idle copy of production alongside the live one costs real infrastructure capacity, which canary's gradual, resource-light shift avoids.

questions.q: In the Istio example, what changes between a canary traffic split and a blue-green cutover using the same VirtualService resource?
options: Blue-green requires a completely different Kubernetes resource type
The usage pattern: canary ramps a weight gradually across many updates, while blue-green flips the weight from 0/100 to 100/0 in a single update
Blue-green cannot use weighted routing at all
Canary only works with Kubernetes Services, never Istio
questions.explain: The same VirtualService weighting mechanism is used for both strategies — the difference is entirely in how gradually the weight is changed.
